title: 105. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Solving Inverse Proportion Problems
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the equation that represents an inverse proportion relationship.
questions.question: If \(y\) is inversely proportional to \(x\), with \(x\ne 0\) and a nonzero constant \(k\), which equation represents the relationship?
questions.explanation: In an inverse proportion, the product of the two variables is constant, so \(xy=k\). Rearranging gives \(y=\frac{k}{x}\). The equation \(y=kx\) represents direct proportion, not inverse proportion.
questions.hint: Decide whether the ratio or the product of the two variables stays constant.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the constant of inverse proportionality from a pair of values.
questions.question: If \(y\) is inversely proportional to \(x\), and \(y=6\) when \(x=4\), what is the constant of proportionality?
questions.explanation: For inverse proportion, \(xy=k\). Substitute \(x=4\) and \(y=6\): \(4\times 6=24\). Therefore, the constant of proportionality is \(24\). The alternative uses the direct-proportion quotient \(\frac{6}{4}=1.5\), rather than the inverse-proportion product.
questions.hint: Keep track of the constant product rather than a constant ratio.

questions.learningObjective: Solve a worker-time problem using inverse proportion.
questions.question: Six identical workers complete a job in \(10\text{ days}\). Each worker works at the same constant rate. With no change in efficiency, how many days will \(12\) workers take to complete the same job?
questions.explanation: The total work is \(6\times 10=60\) worker-days. With \(12\) workers, the time needed is \(60\div 12=5\text{ days}\). The alternative \(20\text{ days}\) scales time in the same direction as the workforce, using \(10\times\frac{12}{6}\).
questions.hint: Keep track of the constant product rather than a constant ratio.

questions.learningObjective: Solve a fixed-distance speed-time problem using inverse proportion.
questions.question: A car travels a fixed distance. At \(60\text{ km/h}\), the trip takes \(4\text{ h}\). At \(80\text{ km/h}\), how long will the trip take?
questions.explanation: The fixed distance is \(60\times 4=240\text{ km}\). At \(80\text{ km/h}\), the time is \(240\div 80=3\text{ h}\). The alternative scales time in the same direction as speed: \(4\times\frac{80}{60}=\frac{16}{3}\text{ h}\).
questions.hint: Identify the fixed total shared by the two changing quantities.

questions.learningObjective: Determine a missing value in an inverse proportion.
questions.question: If \(y\) is inversely proportional to \(x\), and \(y=12\) when \(x=5\), what is \(y\) when \(x=15\)?
questions.explanation: For inverse proportion, \(xy=k\). Here, \(k=12\times 5=60\). When \(x=15\), \(y=60\div 15=4\). The alternative scales \(y\) in the same direction as \(x\): \(12\times\frac{15}{5}=36\).
questions.hint: Consider whether increasing one quantity should increase or decrease the other.

questions.learningObjective: Solve a fixed-area rectangle problem using inverse proportion.
questions.question: A rectangle has a fixed area of \(72\text{ cm}^2\). When its length is \(9\text{ cm}\), its width is \(8\text{ cm}\). If the length becomes \(12\text{ cm}\), what is the width?
questions.explanation: The area is fixed, so length and width are inversely proportional. The constant is \(9\times 8=72\). When the length is \(12\text{ cm}\), the width is \(72\div 12=6\text{ cm}\). The alternative adds the length increase directly to the width, \(8+(12-9)=11\), which would not preserve the area.
questions.hint: Keep track of the constant product rather than a constant ratio.

questions.learningObjective: Solve a tap-time problem using inverse proportion.
questions.question: Four identical taps fill a tank in \(45\text{ min}\). Each tap has the same constant flow rate. With no change in total capacity, how long will six taps take to fill the same tank?
questions.explanation: The total work is \(4\times 45=180\) tap-minutes. With \(6\) taps, the time is \(180\div 6=30\text{ min}\). The alternative \(67.5\text{ min}\) scales time in the same direction as the number of taps: \(45\times\frac{6}{4}=67.5\).
questions.hint: Identify the fixed total shared by the two changing quantities.

questions.learningObjective: Solve a food-supply problem using inverse proportion.
questions.question: A fixed food supply lasts \(18\text{ days}\) for \(20\) people. At the same daily ration, how long will it last for \(30\) people?
questions.explanation: The total food is \(20\times 18=360\) person-days. For \(30\) people, the supply lasts \(360\div 30=12\text{ days}\). The alternative \(27\text{ days}\) scales duration in the same direction as the number of people: \(18\times\frac{30}{20}=27\).
questions.hint: Consider whether increasing one quantity should increase or decrease the other.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the new value of one variable when the other variable changes in an inverse proportion.
questions.question: Two quantities are inversely proportional. When \(x=8\), \(y=10\). What is \(y\) when \(x=16\)?
questions.explanation: For inverse proportion, \(xy=k\). Here, \(k=8\times 10=80\). When \(x=16\), \(y=80\div 16=5\). The alternative \(20\) scales the second quantity in the same direction as the first, rather than keeping their product fixed.
questions.hint: Keep track of the constant product rather than a constant ratio.

questions.learningObjective: Solve a multi-stage work problem involving inverse proportion.
questions.question: A project requires a fixed total amount of work. All machines work at the same constant rate, and adding machines does not change their efficiency. Six machines would take \(15\text{ days}\) to complete it. After \(5\text{ days}\), \(4\) more machines are added. How many total days are needed to finish the project?
questions.explanation: The total work is \(6\times 15=90\) machine-days. In the first \(5\text{ days}\), \(6\) machines complete \(6\times 5=30\) machine-days. The remaining work is \(90-30=60\) machine-days. With \(6+4=10\) machines, the remaining time is \(60\div 10=6\text{ days}\). Thus the total time is \(5+6=11\text{ days}\). The alternative \(9\text{ days}\) assumes all ten machines were available from the start, \(\frac{90}{10}=9\), ignoring the first five days with only six machines.
questions.hint: Calculate the work completed before the extra machines arrive.
